roles.name: Centrelink payment nominee
roles.summary: A person or organisation appointed in writing by the Secretary (through Services Australia) to receive some or all of a person's Centrelink payments. Payment to the nominee counts as payment to the person. The appointment needs the nominee's written consent and must take the person's wishes into account. It does not depend on the person lacking capacity.

assigned.event: Secretary appoints the nominee in writing and directs that all or part of a payment go to the nominee. The nominee must consent in writing, and the principal's wishes must be considered. In practice the principal and nominee set it up jointly, online or by form.

starts.event: When the written appointment and payment direction are in force. A copy goes to both the nominee and the principal.

ends.event: Nominee tells the Secretary in writing they no longer wish to act. The Secretary must revoke as soon as practicable, effective from a later day named in the revocation.
Principal cancels the voluntary arrangement (myGov, phone or service centre)
Secretary revokes after the nominee reports a change in circumstances in response to a s 123K notice, or fails to comply with a s 123K/123L notice (e.g. a statement of how money was spent)

Death of the principal: the payment stops (final payment for allowees up to the day before death; pensioners are paid for the fortnight of death). After that, the executor or administrator deals with Services Australia. Part 3A has no express termination-on-death provision.

notes.text: Capacity is not a condition. A nominee can be appointed for a fully capable person, and the Act does not tie the appointment to a state guardianship or financial management order.

states.label: Appointment in force; payments directed to nominee's bank account
Appointment suspended by the Secretary; it has no effect under Part 3A
Appointment revoked or cancelled, or the principal has died

transitions.event: Secretary appoints in writing and gives payment direction
conditions: Copies given to nominee and principal

transitions.event: Secretary suspends after a reported change of circumstances or non-compliance with a s 123K/123L notice

conditions: Effective from the later day specified

roles.name: Centrelink correspondence nominee
roles.summary: A person or organisation appointed by the Secretary to deal with Centrelink for a benefit recipient: making claims, receiving notices and meeting most requirements. The same person can be both payment and correspondence nominee. Suspension, revocation and the effect of death work the same way as for a payment nominee.

assigned.event: Secretary appoints the nominee in writing, with the nominee's written consent and after considering the principal's wishes

starts.event: On appointment. From then on the nominee may do any act the benefit recipient may do under social security law (except Part 3A matters, and acts a notice requires the recipient to do personally), and notices may be given to the nominee.

ends.event: Nominee withdraws in writing (mandatory revocation), or Secretary revokes for change of circumstances or non-compliance
Death of the principal: there is no longer a benefit recipient to act for, and Services Australia deals with the executor or administrator. No express statutory termination.

Appointment suspended; no effect under Part 3A

roles.name: My Health Record authorised representative
roles.summary: Someone who acts in place of an adult, whom the System Operator is satisfied cannot make decisions, for everything the My Health Records Act allows. It is first a person authorised under Commonwealth, state or territory law or by a court or tribunal (for example an attorney or guardian), otherwise another appropriate person. While one exists, the recipient cannot act for themselves. Also covers parents of children under 14.

assigned.event: System Operator is satisfied the adult is not capable of making decisions and that the person is authorised under law or a court/tribunal decision (or is otherwise appropriate)

starts.event: At the time the System Operator is so satisfied. The representative may then do anything the Act authorises the recipient to do, and must seek out and follow the recipient's will and preferences.

ends.event: The System Operator is no longer satisfied the adult lacks decision-making capacity. Status exists only 'at a time when' the recipient has an authorised representative.
Death of the healthcare recipient: the System Operator must cancel the registration. Uploaded records are kept (not destroyed) until 30 years after death.

notes.text: Deceased person's record: cancellation on death under s 51(6) is not 'cancellation on request' under s 51(1), so the destruction duty in s 17(3) does not apply. The record is retained until 30 years after death (or 130 years after birth if the date of death is unknown). The Act has no role that lets an executor or next of kin run a deceased person's record.
Section 7A imposes a will-and-preferences duty on both authorised and nominated representatives. It is a supported-decision-making-style standard inside a Commonwealth records statute.

roles.summary: An individual the healthcare recipient chooses by agreement and notifies to the System Operator. They can act on the record within the limits the recipient sets, alongside (not instead of) the recipient.

assigned.event: Recipient and individual agree the individual will be nominated representative, and the recipient notifies the System Operator

starts.event: While the agreement is in force and has been notified. The recipient may still act personally.

ends.event: Agreement no longer in force (e.g. ended by the recipient or representative)
Death of the healthcare recipient: registration cancelled; records retained until 30 years after death

roles.name: Legal personal representative (LPR) of a deceased estate for tax
localNames: trustee of the deceased person's estate
roles.summary: The executor with a grant of probate, or the administrator with letters of administration, whom the ATO deals with as if they were the deceased. They lodge the date-of-death return and estate trust returns and pay the deceased's tax out of the estate. Without a grant, the ATO will help but will not record the person as the authorised LPR.

assigned.event: Named as executor in a will, or appointed administrator by a Supreme Court (state/territory law)

starts.event: On grant of probate or letters of administration and notifying the ATO with the grant; the ATO then records the person as authorised LPR

ends.event: Tax obligations of the deceased and estate discharged and estate distributed (no statutory discharge event in the tax Acts)

notes.text: If no grant is obtained within 6 months after death, the Commissioner may determine the deceased's outstanding tax liabilities, publish notice, and recover from the estate's property instead of dealing with a trustee.

As trustee of the deceased estate, the LPR is answerable for returns in a representative capacity, must retain enough money to pay tax, and is personally liable only to the extent of amounts retained or that should have been retained.

states.label: Executor named in will or intended administrator, no grant; ATO may note the person as managing the estate but information and refunds are restricted
Grant obtained and provided to ATO; recorded as authorised LPR

conditions: Australian grant or resealed in Australia

transitions.event: Tax obligations complete and final distribution made

deceasedPersonalDataProtected.note: The Privacy Act 1988 covers only 'personal information' about an 'individual', meaning a natural person. The OAIC reads this as not including deceased persons, unless the information is also about a living person. The statutory privacy tort (Sch 2) also cannot be brought or continued for a deceased person. Separately, the My Health Records Act requires My Health Record data to be retained for 30 years after death. State health-privacy laws (e.g. NSW Health Records and Information Privacy Act 2002) may protect deceased persons' health information; see state files.

digitalAssetsFiduciaryStatute.name: None enacted. NSW Law Reform Commission Report 147 (2019) recommended a statutory access scheme and a nationally consistent approach. No Commonwealth statute was found in the Federal Register of Legislation.

onlineToolsRecognisedInLaw.note: No Commonwealth statute gives legal effect to platform online-tool designations. Law-reform context only: NSWLRC Report 147.
